Overview: Typhoid fever, often simply called typhoid, is an acute systemic illness characterized by prolonged fever and malaise. It belongs to the enteric fever group, alongside paratyphoid
Symptoms: Typhoid's incubation period spans 6-30 days (average 8-14), allowing silent spread. Week one brings insidious onset: sustained high fever rising stepwise to 39-40°C (102-104°F), chills, severe frontal headache, myalgias, and profound exhaustion. By week two, "typhoid state" emerges: patient apathy, delirium, or muttering confusion. Splenomegaly occurs in 50-75%, with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes.
Causes: *Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi is the sole human pathogen—no animal reservoir exists. Transmission is fecal-oral: infected feces contaminate water/food via poor handwashing, sewage leaks or flies. Asymptomatic carriers (gallbladder colonists) seed outbreaks—famous "Typhoid Mary" infected 50+ in early 1900s
Preventions: Precautions Precaution hinges on "WASH" (water, sanitation, hygiene). Vaccination protects travelers/immunocompromised. Conjugate vaccines (TCV) excel for children, herd immunity potential. Screen/treat carriers

When to See a Doctor: Consult a doctor immediately if you have a fever > 101°F/38.3°C lasting 3+ days, especially after endemic travel (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh). Red flags include diarrhea/constipation, headache, weakness, rose spots, confusion, bloody stools, shock. Children: irritability, poor feeding.
